“But when poetry and poets became numerous, when poets began to make money from their poetry, travel to the markets, and rush to attack people’s honor, the orator came to stand above the poet...”
This account by ʿAmr ibn al-ʿAlāʾ does not describe the historical reality accurately when it presents poetry and oratory as having occupied different ranks at different times.

It is not true that pre-Islamic Arabs needed poetry at one stage in a way that differed from their need for oratory at the same stage. Poetry and oratory performed essentially the same social function during the earlier period he is describing.
Even when poetry was “preserving their achievements, increasing their standing,” and doing all the other things he lists, oratory was doing much the same.

In the earlier pre-Islamic period, well before the rise of Islam, the artistic boundary between poetry and oratory had not yet become clearly defined. Naturally, then, their social functions were not sharply separated either.
There was certainly a functional difference between poetry and public speaking. But when did that difference become clear?

Only at a stage when poetic speech had developed into an art with rules distinct from those of public speaking. The difference was not simply a matter of outward form. Each art had to develop its own internal laws.
That stage came relatively late compared with the earlier period of pre-Islamic Arab society.
In other words, a clear distinction between the rules governing poetry and those governing oratory could appear only after a certain level of social and intellectual development had been reached.

At that point, poetry could emerge as an art based more strongly on personal impulses, aesthetic feeling, and suggestive forms of expression, while oratory could emerge as another kind of art based more strongly on objective intellectual aims, logical organization, and forms of expression whose meaning was comparatively direct.
None of this means, however, that ʿAmr ibn al-ʿAlāʾ’s account is completely without historical value.

If we look past the story he tells on the surface, we can find something else in it: an indirect reflection of a real process of change that was beginning to appear in the culture of the period just before Islam.

I mean the development of the economic and social structures of Arabian society and, more specifically, the movement toward social relationships that were beginning to weaken the purely tribal basis of social conflict, institutions, and divisions.
As this change developed, the relationship between poetry and oratory also began to shift.

This change is what ʿAmr ibn al-ʿAlāʾ saw when he said that poetry and poets had become too numerous, that poets had begun to make a living from poetry, travel to the markets, and attack people’s reputations.
But his description does not explain the phenomenon itself. It is only the form in which the phenomenon appeared to earlier observers.

The deeper change was that, during the general weakening of old tribal relationships, pre-Islamic poetry was beginning to move toward the individual existence of the poet. It was beginning to express the conflict between the poet as an individual personality and the control that tribal relationships exercised over that personality.
The poetry of the pre-Islamic outlaws was one expression of the beginnings of this conflict.
At the same time, the weakening of the old order was also appearing in public speaking.

In speeches such as those attributed to Quss ibn Sāʿida, we find a style that moves away from the traditional role of pre-Islamic oratory as a tool serving the interests of a single closed tribe. These newer speeches began to deal with questions broader than tribal relations—relations that were themselves beginning to lose the conditions that had once allowed them to dominate pre-Islamic society.
The historical conclusion we should draw from what ʿAmr ibn al-ʿAlāʾ tells us is therefore twofold.
First, the change affected oratory as well as poetry.
Second, it reflected a change in the social foundations that shaped the direction of both arts and connected them to the wider movement of social and intellectual development.

Mythology is another cultural marker that cannot reasonably be excluded from the study of any people’s culture. In ancient societies, it was closely connected with all the other forms of cultural life.

Mythology includes mythical or legendary images, stories, epics, characters, and symbols, whether simple or complex. Historically, it represents one form of human awareness at an early stage of its development within the wider process of social development.
Mythology expresses a stage at which human beings relied heavily on direct sensory awareness in their first attempts to explain the natural and social world.
But we need to be careful about what this means.
The sensory character of awareness at that early stage was very different from the role of the senses in more developed societies.

Sensory experience is a natural part of human awareness and one of its permanent capacities. Human beings continue to use it in creative activity—in literature and art, and even in other forms of knowledge—no matter how advanced their society becomes.
But this creative capacity itself develops as human history develops.

What we might call sensibility is a way of discovering and seeing, even when it takes the form of an unconscious kind of vision. Its power to discover and see grows as human knowledge and experience grow. In other words, it develops as the conscious mind accumulates knowledge and experience through the material and cultural development of society.

For this reason, the sensibility of a poet today is fundamentally different from that of a medieval poet. The sensibility of a medieval poet was, in turn, different from that of a poet in ancient times, including a poet in pre-Islamic Arabia.

A modern poet draws, even at the level of sensibility, on the accumulated knowledge of many historical periods and on an entire system of modern achievements. The modern poet therefore has a capacity for discovery and insight that cannot be compared with that available to poets in ancient societies.

We say all this because, when discussing mythology as one feature of pre-Islamic Arab culture, we need to recognize something very simple: it was perfectly natural for the Arabs of that period to have this historical form of awareness.
Their mythology reflected the strongly sensory character of awareness at that stage.

The Arabs were no exception among the peoples of the world. Like other peoples, they had a mythology in their ancient history. Pre-Islamic Arab mythology had its own distinctive features, shaped by the particular history of Arab society at the time.
Even mythical material borrowed from peoples with whom the Arabs came into contact took on the characteristics of the society of the Arabian Peninsula.

Pre-Islamic Arab mythology expressed the attempts of this particular kind of tribal society to reach beyond what could immediately be perceived by the senses and to explain features of the universe that people at the time could not yet explain rationally in any other way.

They looked, for example, at natural phenomena that had a powerful and direct effect on their lives: the changing seasons, the alternation between fertile years and drought, the movement of the sun and moon between day and night, the changing positions of the stars, and the apparent permanence of some stars in the same place.
They also faced questions that could not be reduced to directly observable physical things: poetic “inspiration,” death, the passing away of life, and the continuation of existence.
They were equally struck by events in tribal warfare, such as unexpected victories and defeats that could not be explained by what they had materially expected to happen.
Because they did not yet possess a developed rational framework for understanding such things, they explained them mainly through this immediate, sensory form of awareness.
Myths and legends gave expression to that way of seeing the world.

These explanations took the form of unseen beings such as jinn and devils. They said, for example, that every poet had a devil who inspired his poetry. They even assigned particular devils to particular poets, giving each one a name and a set of characteristics.
They also told stories about the miraculous deeds of famous warriors.
And they sometimes explained great natural events by giving extraordinary powers to weak animals. One story, for example, said that the collapse of the Maʾrib Dam was caused by:
“red rats digging into the dam and searching with their feet, pulling loose a rock that a hundred men could not lift, and then pushing it away with the claws of their feet...”
One striking feature of pre-Islamic Arab mythology is the way it gives a sensory and physical form to abstract meanings.

To express the idea of poetic inspiration, for example, people imagined it as a particular being: a “devil.” They then gave this devil human physical qualities—things that could be seen, touched, and heard.
Likewise, to express meanings such as heroism, terror, beauty, ugliness, cruelty, and so on, they might imagine a jinn, a female jinn, a ghoul, a saʿlā, or some similar being.
These beings did not exist as visible creatures in the ordinary world, of course. But in the mythological imagination, they were still given human qualities.

The same was true of the supernatural forces people imagined behind natural phenomena. They pictured these forces as living beings with bodies, emotions, desires, attitudes, and actions like those of human beings.

We can see this in the way they imagined relations among the heavenly bodies and the influence of those bodies on human life, in their worship of natural phenomena themselves, and in the relationships they imagined between themselves and the idols and sacred objects—the gods they had made with their own hands.
This feature of pre-Islamic Arab mythology had a real historical basis in the level of development reached by human awareness at the time.

The consciousness of a polytheistic tribal community had not yet developed to the point where it could easily understand questions about the universe in purely abstract terms. It could not yet separate ideas and meanings completely from their physical and sensory connections with the world.
But this feature also had a history of its own, connected with the history of polytheism in the Arabian Peninsula.
The strongly sensory forms we still find in Arab mythology during the final pre-Islamic period were therefore a continuation of a much older tradition.
At the same time, however, a new development was beginning to appear in the period just before Islam. It would eventually move beyond this deeply rooted polytheistic outlook.
New features were beginning to emerge within pre-Islamic Arab awareness itself. They were developing at a pace that is striking even from our point of view today.
The most important of these changes was a movement toward a view of the world that went beyond immediate sensory forms and entered a limited realm of abstraction.
Naturally, this new development still appeared through mythological forms and remained mixed with older mythological traditions.
Its clearest expression was the way some pre-Islamic Arabs began to think about God.

Their understanding was beginning to move beyond the physical and sensory forms of polytheistic worship toward something more abstract: the idea of divinity as one God existing beyond the world of visible objects.
This gave idols a new position in pre-Islamic religious awareness.

During the final pre-Islamic period, this change also found expression in stories with mythological features about Abraham and his ḥanīf religion of one God. This religion stood in basic opposition to the old polytheism, with its many gods and idols corresponding to the many tribal units that made up pre-Islamic “society.”
Historical study makes it clear that such stories began to circulate among the pre-Islamic Arabs at the same time that the group known as the ḥanīfs was emerging as a new voice.
The ḥanīfs opposed the religious face of pre-Islamic polytheism, including its rituals and forms of worship, and called instead for the religion of Abraham: belief in the one and only God.
This particular development in pre-Islamic awareness was limited and partial, and several factors contributed to it.

Among the most important was the spread of Jewish and Christian beliefs in the main population and economic centers of northwestern Arabia during the sixth century CE, followed by their spread in southern centers as well.
But we must also recognize what was, in reality, the decisive factor: the historical change taking place in the economic and social foundations of pre-Islamic society itself.
Both internal and external forces were creating the material and cultural conditions for this transformation.

The logical outcome was the breaking apart of a society made up of separate tribal units: scattered, closed in on themselves, and caught in destructive struggles for the bare minimum needed to survive—a form of survival that was barely survival at all.
The movement toward breaking apart these separate tribal structures was, in its real historical meaning, a dialectical process of destruction and construction at the same time.
A new society would emerge within a single unifying framework. Across its vast territory, different peoples, cultures, experiences, capacities, and historical traditions would meet and interact.

The society toward which change was already pointing in the final pre-Islamic period would therefore be a society marked by diversity within unity, rather than by the old fragmentation into separate tribal worlds.
E — Signs of Rational Thought among the Pre-Islamic Arabs
We would not normally raise the question in this form. Scientific thinking does not allow us to speak so absolutely about the fixed “nature” of a people’s thought.

But a number of Muslim and European researchers, both earlier and modern, studied certain features of Arab thought at one particular stage of history and then treated those features as permanent racial characteristics.
They took characteristics produced by one historical period and applied them to Arab thought throughout its entire history.

The characteristics of thought among any people or nation reflect the conditions created by the real circumstances of that people’s life. And because the lives of peoples and nations move, change, and develop, the forms of thought that reflect those lives must also move, change, and develop.
They cannot remain fixed and unchanged through every stage of history.

To put the problem more precisely, some researchers looked at Arab thought during the pre-Islamic period and found characteristics that matched the historical conditions of that period. They then concluded that these characteristics defined the nature of Arab thought for all time.
They turned limited judgments into absolute ones and treated them as final truths.
Our objection is not really a defense of some supposed permanent “nature of Arab thought.”
The problem is the method itself.
For us, this is first of all a question of how historical research should be done.
